question: A woman with three consecutive early pregnancy losses is found to have antiphospholipid antibodies on two separate occasions 12 weeks apart. Which treatment regimen is recommended in her next pregnancy to improve live birth rate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspirin alone is insufficient for antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy — it addresses the platelet component but not the hypercoagulable fibrin-clot pathway.
LMWH alone without aspirin is suboptimal. The combination is the evidence-based standard.

answers.text: Low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) plus LMWH once daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The combination of low-dose aspirin and prophylactic-dose LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg/day) from as soon as pregnancy is confirmed is the standard treatment for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome.
Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (warfarin embryopathy) and is contraindicated. LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the single most treatable cause of RPL. Remember: aspirin (antiplatelet) + LMWH (anticoagulant) combination — neither alone is sufficient.
Well reasoned. Aspirin + LMWH together is the only combination shown in RCTs to significantly improve live birth rates in obstetric APS.
